chapter: Playing in New Orleans and influences
title: Colyer's imitation of Bunk, and the lack of American records in England
summary: Colyer copied records indiscriminately; American jazz was kept out of England at the time he left.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You were mentioning Collier's sounding, what, 1949 sounding like an intentionally copy... From Bunk. From Bunk.

Yeah, well, the band was sort of meant to be like Bunk. See, George and Jim Crow both play in styles which I gather is fairly easy to imitate, even if not to, you know, to make it sound like the same, not have the same swing. And it's sort of basically simple stuff. I mean, it's much easier to copy George, I would think, than to copy, I don't know, Johnny Dodd. Nobody would copy Johnny Dodds. But George, you know, I mean, anybody can get that. You know, I can't say this, I can see, they're going to have to edit all this like mad. But anyway, they tried, they tried to imitate George's style. They still do, like mad, everyone wholesale. And that's what they tried to do. Collier, I don't think, ever sounded much like Bunk. He tried to sound like every record he ever heard. He got a bit of Mutt Carey and he got a bit of Percy Humphrey after he got back to, back from New Orleans. And Russell once pointed out to me that what he didn't like about Collier was that he tried to imitate the bad stuff as well as the good stuff. He'd take a record with Kit Howard playing when his lip was terrible, the notes weren't even, you know, the notes were wavering. And Collier would think that was vibrato and very high class and try to play that. And he's got a record of himself doing that. I think that's why Russell doesn't approve him too much. And I think he's largely justified. Except that Russell's one of the few of us who's ever heard the really good men when they were really good. And so he's on an eminence where we have to make do with what we've got, especially if you're stuck in England. And at the time I left England there wasn't any American jazz allowed over there. I mean the Lewis band has been over there a couple of times I think now, but at that time the union was in some terrible deadlock and nobody was allowed to go over there. Cal Collier was filling some kind of a gap. People couldn't even buy most of the records. They're unavailable over there. Still are, the American music records.
Still unavailable over there. They got pirated now and again.

I didn't think all that much of Bunk until I heard Russell's records, until I got over here and heard the American music records. I thought he was just a pretty player, but they were made towards the end, when the band was kind of splitting up, I think.
